title: Rapid comparative evaluation of 2 ambient artificial intelligence applications in a learning health system.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To evaluate ambient Artificial Intelligence (AI) scribe systems (AAS) across multiple domains using a rapid learning health system (LHS) approach, including provider satisfaction, efficiency, documentation quality, usability, and patient sentiment. This LHS evaluation compared 2 AAS systems (Abridge and Nabla) among 100 providers over 90 days. Evaluation incorporated a cluster randomized crossover comparison, analysis of use and EHR-based workflow outcomes, and standardized simulated encounters to assess documentation quality and safety. Outcomes included provider satisfaction, efficiency, note quality, usability, and patient sentiment. In standardized simulated encounters, both systems achieved 76% note element accuracy with minimal risk for harm. In the randomized crossover comparison, Abridge demonstrated higher usability scores (78.5 vs 73) and was preferred 3:1 over Nabla, which had higher automated speech recognition error rates. Across 16 479 clinical encounters, AAS was used in 35.7% of visits. Total EHR time decreased by approximately 5 minutes per day; same-day chart closure increased by approximately 5% during the initial crossover period, but this effect was attenuated. Provider experience was positive (Net Promoter Score [NPS] 53). Both systems demonstrated comparable documentation accuracy and modest efficiency gains while improving clinician satisfaction. Despite similar performance, clinicians reported differences in usability and preference. Adoption below 40% reflected the trade-off between documentation support and verification burden. Rapid, multidimensional evaluation within a LHS can assess AAS across domains of implementation, efficiency, clinician experience, and documentation quality and safety. Ongoing monitoring of efficiency, documentation quality, and use patterns is essential.

title: Challenges in AI based tumor board case summarization and recommendations
desc: Tumor boards, recurring meetings at hospital institutions, assemble cancer specialists (e.g., medical oncology and pathology) to discuss patient care. In this work, we formally define tumor board case summarization, options generation, and meeting outcome prediction as AI tasks. We study datasets from four medical institutions and evaluate state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) from the DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini, and Qwen families using expert human assessment. Medical oncologists created ~9.6k reference texts and 16k human judgments across tasks. Clinicians rated LLM-generated case summaries 3.57–4.59 out of 5.0 across institutions, but recommendation generation remained more challenging, with average scores of 2.0–3.6. Clinical alignment analyses showed modest correlations of ~0.2 for case summarization subtasks and higher correlations of ~0.6 for recommendation generation using LLM-as-Judge metrics. Our proposed TBFact metrics were competitive with LLM-as-Judge approaches in longer prose free-text settings, suggesting a promising direction toward explainable evaluation. This study, to our knowledge the largest expert-grading study of tumor board tasks with both granular and direct assessments, found that criterion-level scores and overall judgments are related nonlinearly. Experts also frequently assigned high ratings to responses that differed substantially from their reference texts, challenging assumptions underlying reference-based automatic evaluation metrics.

title: When does personalization matter? An evidence-to-action beyond smart devices demonstrating the added clinical value of personalization in precision MedTech.
desc: [Personalized medicine] Precision medicine (PM) seeks to improve prevention, diagnosis, and treatment by incorporating biologic, clinical, environmental, and behavioral variation rather than relying exclusively on population averages. Medical technology (MedTech) provides a practical interface through which this approach can be translated into continuous sensing, decision support, and individualized intervention. We use the term personalized/precision medical devices (PMDs) for a conceptual class of devices that combine person-specific inputs with analytics and device-level configuration or adaptation. PMDs overlap with smart devices, connected health, and digital therapeutics, but are distinguished by their explicit coupling of individualized data to clinically meaningful device behavior. This perspective uses a structured narrative literature approach. The literature survey was extended through targeted searches of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and major regulatory/standards sources for publications addressing precision or personalized medicine, biosensing, wearable and implantable devices, point-of-care diagnostics, automated drug delivery, digital therapeutics, artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), interoperability, regulation, cybersecurity, and health equity [Oct. 2025-Oct. 2026]. Preference was given to peer-reviewed clinical studies, systematic reviews, authoritative regulatory guidance, and international standards. Evidence was synthesized narratively around a device lifecycle framework linking individual profile, sensing, data infrastructure, analytics, actuation, clinical workflow, evidence generation, and governance. title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences
desc: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
desc: As clinical AI agents begin to interact with electronic health records (EHRs), large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate their actions. But how reliably can these judges recognize clinically dangerous mistakes, especially when an agent appears to have completed its task successfully? We investigate this question using MedAgentBench by introducing controlled clinical errors into verified agent trajectories. The experiments include 416 faulty trajectories, eight error categories, and six open-weight LLM judges. By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, we measure whether judges genuinely recognize errors rather than simply flagging more actions as unsafe. The findings show that access to clinical evidence significantly improves judge reliability. When shown only the final answer, judges cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged, while flagging 56% of correct trajectories. With full trajectory information, the ability to distinguish unsafe actions from correct ones reaches a score of 0.75, and providing actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39. Surprisingly, including the agent's reasoning does not improve overall performance and reduces detection of incorrectly reported clinical values by 0.18, which remain the hardest errors to detect. MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.

title: Concerns over spillover, exclusions, and hospital unit differences in an AI early warning system trial (CONCERN-EWS)
desc: Rossetti et al. report that hospitalized patients whose care was informed by an AI-based clinical deterioration early warning system (EWS) were 36% less likely to die during a pragmatic cluster-randomized trial when compared to patients on usual care units without the EWS (adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.53-0.78).1 The authors should be applauded for conducting a trial evaluating the effect of an AI intervention on patient health outcomes; more such trials are needed. Several aspects of the study, however, raise concerns that its findings may not accurately reflect the effect of the EWS. First, spillover effects on availability of scarce intensive care unit (ICU) beds could have led to worse outcomes for patients in the control group. Second, EWS-informed clinical decisions may have led to more frequent exclusion of high-risk patients from the intervention group. Either of these concerns could have led to overestimation of AI benefit. Finally, large pre-trial differences in hospital unit mortality rates suggest that unreported cluster-level imbalance or between-cluster variance could also have affected trial results.

title: An AI agent guides a pipeline for selective protein interaction inhibitors from discovery across targets to preclinical evaluation
desc: A protein can engage multiple partners, making it challenging to disrupt disease-associated interactions while preserving others. We developed Bivexia, an AI agent that guides a multistage pipeline from discovery and de novo design through preclinical evaluation. Its decision rules are fixed in advance, and each prospective selection by the agent is cryptographically committed before testing. The objective is to discover small molecules that disrupt specified interactions of a target protein while preserving others. A compound advanced by Bivexia bound LAG-3 with nanomolar affinity and disrupted its interactions with tau and amyloid-{beta} while preserving binding to MHC class II and FGL1. It reduced tau and amyloid-{beta} burden in independent cohorts across two mouse models. The same rules gave three of nine hits on PrP and two of nine on LRP1, none in random controls. Our findings establish a framework for AI agents to pursue defined interaction selectivity across targets.

title: VoxelSlicer: Adaptive Voxel-wise Slicer for Deformable Image Registration.
source: PubMed · IEEE transactions on medical imaging
desc: [IEEE transactions on medical imaging] Recent progress in neural networks has accelerated deformable image registration (DIR) by amortizing iterative optimization, offering faster results and potential accuracy gains with label supervision. However, existing methods struggle with highly deformed structures (e.g., inter-subject abdominal or intra-subject cardiac scans) and fail to handle complex motions like sliding or respiratory dynamics. This limitation arises from isotropic diffusive pair-wise regularization, which leads to inefficient message passing and oversmoothed boundaries. We propose VoxelSlicer, a novel neural network module inspired by the traditional bilateral grid but enhanced with learnable adaptive filtering. VoxelSlicer enables voxel-wise adaptive filtering, addressing local discontinuities in displacement fields and performs more efficient message passing. This design enables adaptive displacement-cost propagation with a compact parameter footprint and a favorable accuracy-complexity trade-off. Experiments on four realistic datasets and two synthetic datasets with different modalities and input constraints demonstrate VoxelSlicer's competitive registration performance together with favorable accuracy-complexity and accuracy-smoothness trade-offs.

title: AI-assisted chest CT scan analysis of body composition at ICU admission and 6-month mortality
desc: Abnormal body composition at intensive care unit (ICU) admission is associated with worse survival, but it is rarely measured in practice because manual CT analysis is labor-intensive. We conducted a secondary analysis of a single-center prospective cohort of 509 patients who underwent chest CT within 24 h of ICU admission, of whom 475 were included in the final analysis. Open-source AI segmentation was used to quantify body composition, and the resulting features were related to 6-month survival. Risk scores derived from body composition were significantly associated with 6-month survival ( p < 0.001, log-rank test). In five-fold cross-validation, the AUC for discriminating survivors from non-survivors was 0.73; when feature selection was accounted for, the AUC was 0.68 by nested cross-validation and 0.69 by bootstrap optimism correction. The study shows that the automated AI-based analysis of admission chest CT yields body composition scores significantly associated with 6-month mortality after ICU admission.

title: Artificial intelligence and enhanced recovery after surgery: from protocol-driven pathways to adaptive perioperative care systems (cognitive ERAS).
desc: [Minerva anestesiologica] Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) programs have transformed perioperative care through standardized, evidence-based pathways, improving outcomes across surgical specialties. However, increasing patient complexity and heterogeneity expose important limitations of protocol-driven approaches, which often fail to capture dynamic physiological variability and individualized recovery trajectories. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a pathway to overcome these constraints by integrating longitudinal perioperative data and generating individualized risk predictions. However, prediction alone is insufficient for clinically meaningful personalization, which requires causal reasoning to estimate which interventions are most likely to improve outcomes for specific patients and at different stages of recovery. In this context, ERAS may evolve toward a data-informed, adaptive care system that integrates prediction, causal inference, and supervised workflow coordination. Emerging agentic AI systems may further extend ERAS beyond passive decision support toward structured care orchestration within defined clinical governance boundaries. This review examines how different AI methodologies, including supervised learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, generative models, and causal inference, can be aligned with ERAS objectives across the perioperative continuum. We also critically evaluate current evidence and key barriers to implementation. Looking forward, the convergence of AI, digital health technologies, and continuous patient monitoring may enable the emergence of cognitive ERAS, a data-driven perioperative care model that integrates prediction, causal estimation, and continuous learning to deliver personalized and dynamically adaptive recovery pathways.

title: Evaluating the Feasibility of an Artificial-Intelligence Based Clinical Decision Support Tool for People With Chronic Lung Disease
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: University of Pennsylvania; conditions: Population Health Management, Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS), Chronic Lung Diseases, Artificial Intelligence (AI); type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 45; status: RECRUITING] Patients living with chronic lung diseases (CLD) are at high risk of frailty, malnutrition, and depression. However, many of the interventions targeting these conditions are underutilized. Thus, artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) offer a promising approach to guide targeted interventions for this population and reduce risk of hospitalization. The purpose of this study is to assess the acceptability and feasibility of a new AI-CDSS for community-dwelling patients with CLD. The goal of this AI-CDSS is to predict the probability that patients would benefit from 5 frailty- and depression-focused interventions (pulmonary rehabilitation, physical therapy, fall-risk assessment, nutrition consultation, and depression consultation). In this study, pulmonologists will review the AI-CDSS's predictions and have the option to recommend referrals for their patients. If a referral is recommended, the study team will contact the patient to discuss the referral and start the referral process. All participants will then complete a semi-structured interview and feedback survey asking their opinions about the AI-CDSS and the study referral process.

title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
desc: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.

title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
desc: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

title: Tabular Foundation AI Models in Healthcare: A WHO-Inspired Benchmark for Responsible AI and Trustworthiness
desc: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly used for structured prediction, yet their suitability for healthcare applications remains uncertain because predictive performance alone does not establish fairness, probabilistic reliability, or robustness. We developed a multidimensional benchmark to compare four TFMs: TabFM, TabPFN, TabDPT, and TabICL, against Logistic Regression and XGBoost across a curated, standardized suite of ten WHO-aligned healthcare classification datasets across diverse disease domains. Additionally, we harmonized clinical schemas, standardized protected sex attributes and outcome targets, and released both balanced-scale and natural-prevalence variants of the datasets to establish a benchmarking resource in healthcare machine learning. All models were evaluated using identical five-fold stratified cross-validation partitions and standardized preprocessing. Performance was assessed using 20 metrics spanning predictive discrimination, sex-based fairness, probability calibration, and robustness to Gaussian feature perturbations. A composite Clinical Model Evaluation Score (CMES) was used to summarize performance across these dimensions. Google TabFM achieved the highest mean CMES (0.8811), followed closely by TabDPT (0.8796), TabICL (0.8775), TabPFN (0.8756), XGBoost (0.8650), and Logistic Regression (0.8549). The Friedman test indicated significant differences among models ({chi}2F (5) = 24.914, p = 1.45 x 10^-4; Kendalls W = 0.498). However, post-hoc comparisons revealed no statistically significant differences among the four TFMs after Holm correction. TFMs generally demonstrated stronger discrimination and probabilistic calibration than conventional baselines, with TabFM achieving the highest mean Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (0.9327) and the lowest expected calibration error (0.0674). Conversely, Logistic Regression exhibited the greatest stability under feature perturbations, while fairness performance varied substantially across datasets and models. These findings highlight the potential of TFMs for small-data healthcare prediction while demonstrating that their advantages are dimension-dependent. Multidimensional, dataset-specific evaluation and external validation remain essential before clinical implementation. All analysis codes, original datasets, and multiple variants of benchmark datasets are publicly available in a GitHub repository to ensure reproducibility and future research.

title: CheekAI: An explainable, deep learning epigenetic aging clock based on lifestyle and health epigenetic biomarker proxies
desc: The human methylome is poorly understood and, as such, the vast majority of epigenetic aging clocks are unexplainable black boxes. To address this, we created CheekAI, a robust deep learning model that uses lifestyle and health epigenetic biomarker proxies (EBPs) to predict age. Trained using a longitudinal dataset of 25,400 adult buccal DNA methylation samples derived from 14,716 distinct adults, we used principal components and multi-objective optimization to produce a clock that is explainable, reproducible, responsive, and accurate. The Pearson correlation with chronological age is 0.969, the mean absolute error is 2.49 years, and the intraclass correlation coefficient across 679 replicate pairs is 0.990. CheekAI was significantly associated with a plethora of lifestyle and health variables, including resting heart rate, omega-3 intake, ultra-processed food intake, daily step count, resistance training, and time spent in nature. When applied to external saliva and buccal datasets, CheekAI significantly captured a variety of signals, including smoking and oesophageal cancer. CheekAI was also significantly reduced by a multifactorial lifestyle intervention and this reduction was driven by improvements in dietary and metabolic EBPs. This novel artificial intelligence model represents the first instance of a buccal epigenetic aging clock that utilizes EBPs to offer interpretability and actionability.

title: Multimodal AI-enabled repurposing and prioritization of ferroptosis-targeting drug combinations in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
desc: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) lacks scalable and mechanism-informed computational strategies for prioritizing repurposable drug combinations. Here, we developed FeNetDP, a multimodal AI-guided framework that integrates transcriptomic, proteomic, single-cell, spatial, and clinical survival data to enable biologically grounded drug repurposing and combination prioritization in PDAC. FeNetDP combines gene-level network proximity analysis with a biologically constrained neural ranking model to identify candidate compounds and drug pairs linked to a disease-relevant ferroptosis suppressor program. Using this framework, we defined an eight-gene ferroptosis suppressor module enriched in ductal cells and associated with poor prognosis, and prioritized candidate repurposable compounds and combinations targeting this network state. Prospective experimental validation identified panobinostat plus sorafenib as a synergistic combination that suppresses tumor growth and promotes ferroptosis in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, the combination impaired ferroptosis resistance through coordinated disruption of glutathione-dependent antioxidant defense and AIFM2 (FSP1)-associated glutathione-independent protection. Together, these findings establish FeNetDP as a multimodal and experimentally grounded framework for computational repurposing and mechanism-informed therapeutic prioritization in cancer.

title: Evaluation of Large Language Model Chatbots as Patient Education Resources for Glioma: A Comparative Study.
source: PubMed · Journal of cancer education : the official journal of the American Association for Cancer Education
desc: [Journal of cancer education : the official journal of the American Association for Cancer Education] Patients and caregivers increasingly consult large language model (LLM) chatbots for glioma-related information. Explaining glioma requires discussion of tumor classification, molecular pathology, treatment, and prognosis, making accurate patient education challenging. However, the quality of glioma-related information generated by LLMs has not been systematically evaluated. To compare the quality, transparency, and readability of glioma-related information generated by four publicly accessible LLM chatbots and assess whether their responses meet recommended readability standards for patient education. In this cross-sectional study, Google Trends was used to identify commonly searched glioma-related topics. Seventeen patient-oriented questions derived from 19 search terms were submitted to ChatGPT 5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Microsoft Copilot, and Perplexity. Two independent reviewers assessed response quality using DISCERN, Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmark criteria, and the Global Quality Score (GQS). Readability was evaluated using six validated indices. Group differences were analyzed with the Kruskal-Wallis test followed by Dunn-Bonferroni post hoc comparisons. Significant differences were observed among the four chatbots for DISCERN (P = 0.001), EQIP (P < 0.001), JAMA (P < 0.001), and GQS (P = 0.022). Copilot achieved the highest DISCERN and EQIP scores, whereas ChatGPT received the highest GQS. Copilot and Perplexity demonstrated better transparency than ChatGPT and Gemini, although overall transparency remained limited. None of the chatbots met recommended readability standards for patient education. Publicly accessible LLM chatbots can provide structured glioma-related information, but performance varies across platforms. Limited transparency and poor readability restrict their suitability as stand-alone patient education tools. Improvements in evidence attribution, guideline-based retrieval, uncertainty communication, and plain-language adaptation are needed before routine use in neuro-oncology.

title: AI-Assisted Adaptive Support to Reduce Post-Intensive Care Syndrome-Family
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Baqiyatallah Medical Sciences University; conditions: Post-Intensive Care Syndrome-Family (PICS-F), Post-Traumatic Stress, Psychological Distress; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 1000; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The ASSIST trial evaluates whether an AI-assisted smartphone application can reduce post-traumatic stress symptoms and other psychological distress in family members of critically ill patients. Admission to an intensive care unit (ICU) places a severe psychological burden on families, often leading to post-intensive care syndrome-family (PICS-F). Current support is mostly reactive and rarely available after the patient is discharged. This study is a three-center randomized controlled trial involving 1000 family members. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either standard care or standard care plus the ASSIST smartphone platform. During the ICU stay, the platform uses an artificial intelligence model to simplify clinical information (approved by a clinician) and helps families prepare questions for the medical team. After the patient is discharged, the platform monitors the family member's mood daily. If a risk of anxiety or depression is detected, it provides a brief digital cognitive behavioral therapy module. The main goal is to see if the ASSIST platform reduces post-traumatic stress over a 12-month period compared to standard care alone. Secondary goals include evaluating its effects on acute stress, decisional conflict, anxiety, depression, and caregiver burden. The study will also include qualitative interviews to understand the family members' lived experiences using the platform

title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
desc: The decay exponent α in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as s_i = A_i cdot (t-i)^{-α}, where A_i is cumulative attention and α controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to α=0 and αtoinfty, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of xiang2026nohair bounds the admissible range of α, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields [0.556, 0.822] for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. NoHairCache achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p < 0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
desc: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.

title: Leveraging HCUP Data to Predict Preventable Admissions in Patients with Chronic Kidney Diseases
desc: Objectives: This study developed machine learning (ML) to predict 90-day preventable admissions in CKD patients while evaluating racial disparities in model performance. Materials and Methods: Study population included CKD patients (above 18 years) with hospital encounters in Maryland (2016-2023). Logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), XGBoost, and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) models were used to predict 90-day preventable admissions after a CKD outpatient visit. Data used in this study was extracted from Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP). Results: 28,214 unique patients were included, of whom 3974 (14%) experienced a subsequent preventable admission. LR achieved comparable performance with RF and XGBoost (AuROC 0.784 - 0.788, AuPRC 0.397 - 0.416), outperforming KNN (AuROC 0.753, AuPRC 0.342). All models performed marginally better in the Black population (AuROC 0.773 - 0.807, AuPRC 0.369 - 0.467) than in the white population (AuROC 0.738 - 0.776, AuPRC 0.329 - 0.394). The false negative rates (FNR) in the white population were higher across different models (Black: 0.236 - 0.33, white: 0.297 - 0.377). Discussion: Our results suggest that LR can achieve comparable prediction performances than tree-based ML algorithms. Hospital utilization and congestive heart failure are among the most important predictors across models. Further analyses on prediction bias revealed that FNRs are more significant in white patients, which can be due to their overall lower utilization. Conclusions: This study demonstrated a pipeline to develop ML models predicting preventable admissions while revealing existing racial biases. These findings can inform ambulatory settings on how to reduce preventable admissions among CKD patients.

title: Multi-omics causal deep learning reveals regulatory structure while interventions refine perturbation predictions
desc: Inferring gene regulation from single-cell data is difficult because observational measurements cannot distinguish correlation from causation and access to perturbational data, especially with multiple modalities, remains limited. Here we present the Cross-Modal Causal Variational Autoencoder (CMC-VAE), which learns a network linking genes and proteins (gene-gene, protein-protein and gene-protein) in the latent space and maps each connection back onto measured features. Trained on 809,130 observational CITE-seq profiles, CMC-VAE recovers co-expression, transcription factor regulons and immune signalling programs, and learns a sparse cross-modal map enriched for transcript-protein cognate pairs. On three CRISPR screens used during development, it ranks knockout-responsive genes better than correlation and latent-VAE baselines. Fitted to a screen's unperturbed control cells, without perturbation labels, the model translates measured knockout RNA responses into protein responses better than a correlation map and cognate transcripts. The direction of gene-to-gene regulation, however, is not recovered from observational data. On the CITE-seq screens, fine-tuning only the latent network improves held-out response correlation, mainly by learning a response shared across knockouts. On larger Perturb-seq screens, with about 1,000 training perturbations, fine-tuning the latent network learns gene-specific effects that transfer to held-out genes, more so than a gene-level causal model fine-tuned on the same cells, and in simulation, such interventions also restore edge orientations that observational training leaves unresolved.

title: Large Language Models for Electronic Health Records in Emergency Department (ED) and ED-Adjacent Emergency Care-Technical Strategies, Clinical Tasks, and Workflow Integration: Systematic Review.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in clinical text processing, but their role in emergency departments (EDs) and ED-adjacent emergency care remains unclear because ED electronic health records (EHRs) are heterogeneous, time-critical, and safety-sensitive. This study aims to synthesize peer-reviewed evidence on LLM applications to real-world ED EHR data and ED-adjacent emergency care data, focusing on clinical tasks, technical strategies, evaluation practices, and workflow integration. We conducted a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)-guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (January 1, 2022, to November 14, 2025). We included peer-reviewed English-language studies applying LLM strategies to ED and ED-adjacent EHR data. We extracted dataset characteristics, model families, task formulations (classification, summarization, and information extraction), adaptation strategies (prompting, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic/hybrid workflows), evaluation metrics, and ED workflow phase. Two reviewers also independently completed a design-matched methodological quality and risk-of-bias appraisal. Thirty-one studies met our inclusion criteria. Many relied on single-center datasets (n=12), relatively small sample sizes (<10,000 encounters; n=20), and English-language unstructured text alone or mixed EHR inputs combining text with structured or semistructured fields. Prompt engineering was the dominant adaptation strategy (n=27), while fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and hybrid/agentic pipelines were less common. Postencounter studies frequently demonstrated task-specific retrospective technical feasibility, while triage, diagnostic-support, and disposition studies evaluated heterogeneous tasks and outcomes; these nonequivalent measures were not compared as indicators of workflow maturity. Workflow-phase assignment did not imply real-time integration, particularly when model inputs were available only after the relevant clinical decision point. Overall, 22 (71%) studies were classified as technical-performance-only evaluations; clinical utility was empirically assessed in only 3 (9.7%) studies, and prospective deployment in 4 (12.9%). No study directly measured patient outcomes or downstream patient-safety outcomes attributable to LLM use. title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
desc: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

title: Evaluating Prominent Machine Translation Models for Kinyarwanda to English for Patient-Provider Conversations
desc: Background Linguistic barriers between patients and providers cause diagnostic error, poor adherence, and adverse events, and disproportionately affect speakers of low-resource languages. Kinyarwanda, spoken by more than 20 million people, has a small digital footprint, and the quality of off-the-shelf machine translation (MT) for its clinical dialogue is poorly documented. Methods We evaluated six MT systems (GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Azure Translate, Google Translate, and NLLB-200) for Kinyarwanda-to-English patient-provider conversations. Using a professional reference corpus of 600 conversations, stratified across three pandemic periods and collected in Rwanda via the WelTel platform, we assessed automated metrics (semantic similarity, BLEU, chrF, and translation edit rate [TER]) and 0-100 quality ratings from three professional Kinyarwanda-English translators, with reliability quantified by intraclass correlation (ICC). De-identified secondary data were approved by UBC (H20-01031) and the Rwanda National Ethics Committee (100/RNEC/2020). Findings On the full 600-conversation cohort, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5, and Gemini 2.5 Flash had closely clustered semantic similarity (0.877, 0.874, 0.873), well above Azure Translate (0.809) and NLLB-200 (0.754); Gemini 2.5 Flash led on BLEU (43.13) and the lowest TER (68.15). Translators ranked GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash highest (means 81.55 and 81.51), then GPT-4o-mini (72.67), Azure Translate (55.16), and NLLB-200 (39.05); average-rater reliability was moderate (ICC 0.594, rising to 0.701 on a balanced 85-conversation subset). Automated n-gram metrics understated the quality gap human raters perceived between large language models and conventional systems. Interpretation GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Flash are the strongest off-the-shelf systems for Kinyarwanda-English clinical translation and primary choices for human-in-the-loop use, with GPT-4o-mini a cost-efficient alternative. NLLB-200 underperformed, showing that models built for low-resource languages are not automatically suited to specialised clinical domains without fine-tuning. Human evaluation should be prioritised over automated metrics alone when comparing LLM-based translation.

title: Deciphering Molecular Language for Spectral Interpretation with a Foundation Model Pretrained on Repository-Wide Metabolomics Data
desc: In-depth, scalable structural interpretation of tandem mass spectra from diverse biological tissues and environmental samples is essential for understanding the molecular diversity of cellular environments and the metabolic architecture of living systems. Although community-driven resources such as GNPS and MassIVE have aggregated massive volumes of tandem mass spectra spanning a wide range of organisms, clinical cohorts and environmental surveys, modeling and interpreting this exponentially expanding spectral corpus to distill molecular information and derive meaningful biological insights poses a fundamental challenge for established computational methods. Here we present UltraMS, a dual-polarity foundation model tailored to decipher the molecular language latent in tandem mass spectra through large-scale pretraining on more than 160 million spectra encompassing both positive and negative ion modes. Our findings illustrate that UltraMS is capable of effectively decoding the chemical semantics of molecules underlying mass spectra via self-supervised learning, achieving superior performance across a variety of downstream tasks, including elemental detection, molecular identification, molecular property profiling, and metabolic landscape characterization. Remarkably, UltraMS enables conducting molecular identification with fine-grained spectral interpretability, simultaneously elucidating molecular structures from untargeted MS/MS spectra and providing peak-by-peak substructural attributions via annotation transfer. Deployed on a clinical cohort of human plaque samples, UltraMS demonstrates significant potential in discovering previously unrecognized phenotype-linked metabolites supported by structurally grounded fragment-ion formation pathways, while effectively correcting likely misannotated clinical markers. Furthermore, building on the structure-aware spectral representations learned by UltraMS, we construct UltraAtlas, a chemical-property-resolved map that organizes millions of experimental spectra into a unified coordinate system, enabling millisecond-scale molecular profiling and offering practical guidance for exploratory navigation across vast chemical space. Applied to human scalp metabolomics, UltraAtlas effectively captures distinct metabolic variations across individuals, highlighting phenotype-specific chemical signatures while shedding light on the chemical niches of the resident microbiome. title: Generative fundus angiography from misaligned handheld images for non-invasive screening of infantile retinal diseases
desc: Infantile retinal diseases are a leading cause of childhood blindness, and vascular findings that guide screening and management are often poorly visible in color fundus photography (CFP). Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) provides angiographic visualization of retinal vascular abnormalities, but its invasive nature and reliance on fluorescein dye limit routine use in vulnerable infants. Generative synthesis may provide non-invasive angiographic approximations. However, infant imaging often relies on manually operated handheld contact fundus cameras, with variations in probe angle, contact pressure, and field of view between separate CFP and FFA acquisitions contributing to weak spatial correspondence between modalities. In this paper, we present InfantAngio, a diffusion-based framework that reformulates CFP-to-FFA synthesis as a deterministic latent transport trajectory. Developed and evaluated using 83,950 registration-derived image-pair records from 259 infants, InfantAngio showed favorable performance across quantitative image-quality benchmarks, while ophthalmologists distinguished real from synthesized FFA images with near-chance accuracy of 49.8% in blinded assessment. Adding synthesized FFA to CFP improved both downstream classifier performance and overall diagnostic accuracy in a retrospective ophthalmologist reader study. These results support synthesized FFA as a potentially useful non-invasive adjunct for screening high-risk infants, with the possibility of reducing reliance on dye-based procedures in real-world clinical scenarios.

title: A Scoping Review on Large Language Model Clinical Decision Support in Acute and Critical Care.
desc: [Journal of medical systems] Decision-making in acute and critical care relies on interpretation of heterogeneous information sources under substantial time pressure. Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as clinical decision support systems (CDSS) to aid in triage, diagnosis generation, and treatment planning. This scoping review maps the current landscape of LLM-based CDSS in acute and critical care and assesses their readiness for clinical implementation. A PRISMA-ScR-guided search of four databases (January 2026) yielded 62 studies, including 15 medical domain-adapted LLMs. Technology Readiness Levels were assigned across all 62 studies; none has progressed to clinical deployment. Within the medical LLM subgroup, medical LLMs generally outperformed their foundation model counterparts, although the evidence was heterogeneous. An exploratory PROBAST + AI-informed appraisal identified recurring methodological concerns, and thematic synthesis of implementation determinants identified regulatory constraints, workflow integration, and insufficient understanding of human-AI interaction as key barriers. This review highlights priorities for prospective validation using real-world institutional data.

The main questions it aims to answer are: * How safe is an AI chatbot in use for a study about mental wellness? * How usable is the platform for this study? * How willing are participants to remain and complete the study? * What was the user experience like? * Do they show any signs of dependancy on the chatbot? Researchers will compare participants who did the mental wellness sessions with the chosen chatbot, Doro, to those who used common self-help materials to examine the safety and effectiveness of AI chatbots in supporting mental wellness. Participants will: * Have a pre-study mental wellness assessment. * Be divided into 2 groups: the experimental group and the control group. * The experimental group will interact with the Doro AI Chatbot. * The control group will interact with the self-help work materials. * Have a mid-point mental wellness assessment. * Have a mental wellness survey after all the sessions, and * Have a final interview with one of the researchers.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
desc: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: Effect of a feedback loop on clinical prediction model performance
desc: Clinical prediction models (CPMs) that guide treatment-initiation, and therefore affect patient outcomes, may create feedback loops when updated using data from patients whose care they influenced. Treatment can alter predictor-outcome relationships and outcome prevalence, potentially reducing model performance. This simulation study aims to quantify this effect using setting parameters based on cardiovascular disease prediction and intervention and assess if including a treatment variable in the model mitigates any performance degradation. In the simulation, models were developed to predict the probability of a binary adverse outcome, guide treatment allocation, and then updated using data containing patients in whom the model was applied. Scenarios varied treatment inclusion as a predictor in the model and the presence of unmeasured confounding. Performance was assessed with calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, c-statistic, and correct risk assignment relative to treatment threshold. Without unmeasured confounding, excluding treatment as a predictor resulted in miscalibration, but including treatment solves this problem completely. With unmeasured confounding, performance deteriorated even when treatment was included. These results agree with previous findings and illustrate the likelihood that models that guide interventions may experience performance deterioration due to the difficulty of recording treatment and avoiding unmeasured confounders. Causal inference methods combined with risk prediction may help address this problem. Further research is needed on monitoring techniques to allow detection of this issue post-model implementation.

title: BiocPy: A Framework for Cross-Platform Genomic Data andMethods Interoperability
desc: Bioconductor provides standardized data structures and statistical methods for high-throughput genomic analysis in R, whereas Python has become a primary environment for machine learning, image analysis, and general-purpose data science. Combining tools across both ecosystems often requires ad-hoc file conversions or embedded language runtimes that can lose metadata, introduce maintenance overhead, or lead to subtle differences in downstream results. Here, we present BiocPy, a collection of Python packages that support cross-language genomic workflows through three complementary layers: (1) native Python implementations of Bioconductor's core data structures; (2) lossless data exchange via direct reading and writing of serialized R (.rds) objects and the language-neutral ArtifactDB format for persistent, multi-stage pipelines; and (3) a cross-platform method development paradigm built on shared C++ libraries wrapped across R, Python, and WebAssembly to support identical statistical analyses across environments. All packages in the BiocPy ecosystem are published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) with source code hosted at [https://github.com/BiocPy].

Artificial intelligence in epilepsy care: a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical applications in diagnosis, classification, outcome prediction, and surgical decision-making.
desc: [Neurosurgical review] Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, with disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries where access to specialized care remains limited. Despite advances in neuroimaging and electrophysiology, accurate diagnosis, etiological classification, and timely identification of surgical candidates remain major clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to integrate multimodal data and support clinical decision-making across the epilepsy care continuum. Searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Cochrane Library, and SciELO for studies published between January 2014 and March 2026. title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation
desc: As incentives to digitize more and more aspects of medical healthcare are gaining traction, additional medical data is becoming available. A major goal is to use this data to gain further insights, support medical staff, and ultimately improve patient care. This demands sophisticated solutions that can handle current and future vast amounts of data, all without disrupting well-established workflows of care takers. Additionally, the solution must fulfill the documentation and risk-management obligations of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which governs whether a device may be used in patient care in Europe. In this context, we introduce the AMPEL platform, an open-source solution for creating clinical decision support systems (CDSS) that fulfil the requirements of the MDR. Centered around a message broker (Kafka), it adopts an event-driven, distributed architecture, allowing for scaling and efficient processing of medical data as it gets generated. Relying on platform-specific events to implicitly describe the platform's interfaces makes it both extensible and agnostic to the hospital information system in use. With these events being defined in the Protocol Buffers format, medically evaluated algorithms can be independently implemented in a variety of programming languages and easily linked to the platform, extending its analytic capabilities as desired. The platform features a basic UI and alert functionality that can be used to gain medical staff's attention and present analysis results in a traceable and explainable fashion. We further show in a use case how the platform was used to build LAMPE, a CDSS developed and operated at University of Leipzig Medical Center. It demonstrates how the platform solution can be used in a complex and already established environment, while acknowledging current limitations and outlining planned developments to overcome these.

title: Optimizing Sepsis Treatment via Latent Protocol Inference
desc: Sepsis is a life-threatening medical emergency characterized by high mortality and variable treatment practices. Optimizing treatment from retrospective data is challenging due to sparse, delayed outcomes and complex physiological dynamics. We introduce the Generative Latent Protocol Model (GLPM), a probabilistic framework that structures clinical decision-making through a latent protocol variable anchored on the patient's admission state. This latent variable acts as an information bottleneck, decoupling the generation of treatment trajectories from the prediction of survival outcomes. Unlike methods that rely on value estimation or noisy return-to-go conditioning, our model is trained via maximum likelihood estimation to capture the joint distribution of treatment trajectories and outcomes. At inference time, we treat treatment optimization as a probabilistic inverse problem: we sample latent protocols from a posterior distribution conditioned on a target survival probability. On the ICU-Sepsis benchmark derived from MIMIC-III, our best variant matches or exceeds eight offline baselines on all five datasets, with gains that are statistically significant against every baseline on the most heterogeneous dataset, and offers interpretability through patient-specific counterfactual analysis.

title: GlycanPUG: WURCS-Based Heterogeneous Graph Pretraining for Structurally Ambiguous Glycans
desc: Background: Glycans orchestrate diverse biological processes, yet they remain underrepresented in computational biology compared to proteins and nucleic acids. Although WURCS 2.0 provides a machine-readable structural representation that preserves uncertainty, the evaluated IUPAC-based deterministic workflow processes 43.1% of the GlyCosmos-derived cohort examined here, motivating approaches that retain structural ambiguity. Methods: To overcome this limitation, GlycanPUG (Probabilistic Uncertainty-aware Graph) was introduced as a pretrained graph model for glycan representation learning. By leveraging WURCS 2.0, GlycanPUG represents candidate linkages and substituent attachments using weighted edges and uncertainty attributes within a heterogeneous graph framework. A 4-layer Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network with a dedicated node pre-enhancement module aggregates edge features weighted by the assigned edge weights, enabling representation of supported structurally ambiguous glycans without selecting a single resolved structure. The model is pretrained on a preprocessed subset of the GlyTouCan1 repository, which contained 253,596 entries before filtering. After excluding entries linked to downstream tasks and applying sequential structural filtering, 167,020 samples remained and were used for pretraining. Pretraining comprised nine self-supervised tasks. Results: Benchmarking on the GlycanML dataset demonstrates that GlycanPUG shows competitive performance relative to GlycanGT across multi-label taxonomy classification and binary immunogenicity prediction. Crucially, on datasets natively containing structural uncertainties (GlyCosmos, GlyConnect), GlycanPUG effectively processes additional structurally ambiguous entries, achieving 83.5% processable coverage across all glycans from all biological sources in GlyCosmos, with taxonomic classification performance (e.g., mean macro F1 of 0.7376 for Domain). Ablation of the node pre-enhancement module reduces macro F1, and post-hoc analysis identifies rank-dependent associations between structural uncertainty and prediction errors. All results reported above are averaged over ten independent random seeds (1-10). Conclusions: GlycanPUG broadens the set of glycans that can be represented while retaining supported structural ambiguities.

desc: [Pediatric research] The inaugural Pediatric Research Forum for the Future of Children (PRFC), held in Geneva, Switzerland, brought together leading investigators and emerging scientists from across the globe to discuss the future trajectory of pediatric research. Organized collaboratively by the Society for Pediatric Research (SPR) and the European Society for Paediatric Research (ESPR), the meeting was designed to foster international collaboration, highlight transformative research directions, and cultivate the next generation of pediatric clinician-scientists. A distinctive feature of the conference was its paired presentation format, in which established senior investigators presented alongside early-career researchers across five thematic domains: precision medicine and novel therapies, big data in pediatric research, early life determinants of health and disease, child mental health and development, and global pediatric research and workforce development. The meeting emphasized the importance of interdisciplinary science, equitable global partnerships, and translational pathways that accelerate the integration of discoveries into clinical practice. Key insights included the rapid expansion of genomic medicine in pediatrics, the potential and limitations of artificial intelligence and big data, the profound influence of early life exposures on lifelong health trajectories, the urgent need to address pediatric mental health, and the critical role of global collaboration and clinician-scientist training in advancing child health. The PRFC demonstrated that innovative meeting structures and cross-generational dialog can catalyze new research directions and strengthen the pediatric research ecosystem. IMPACT: This article highlights the presentations given at the Inaugural Pediatric Research for the Future of Children, held in Geneva in February, 2026.

title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
desc: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

title: Community pharmacy responses to online reviews: a national cross-sectional study
desc: Objectives: Online reviews constitute a source of information on the experience of users in community pharmacies. The way in which pharmacists engage with them remains poorly documented. The objective was to describe the frequency, determinants, and content of the responses provided by French pharmacy teams to reviews published on Google Maps. Methods: Cross-sectional observational study. Public reviews from nearly all French community pharmacies (approximately 20 000) were collected automatically between September and October 2026. For each review, the rating, the text of the review, the time since its publication, and the text of the response, if it existed, were collected. Factors associated with the response were studied using logistic regression. Sentiment of the reviews and the tone of the responses were automatically coded according to a predefined grid. The presence of reviews generated by artificial intelligence, as well as potential interventions on the ratings, were explored.newline Results: In total, 1 008 024 extractions (729 521 reviews and 278 504 responses) concerning 19 985 pharmacies were analysed. A response was present for 38% of reviews and 67.5% of pharmacies had responded at least once. The response rate was higher for negative reviews (one or two stars) than for positive reviews (five stars) (adjusted OR 1.35; 95% CI [1.33--1.38]; adjusted risk difference +3.6 percentage points; 95% CI [3.3--3.8]), and these responses were approximately twice as long (adjusted geometric mean ratio 3.03; 95% CI [3.01--3.06]). The tone of the responses was very widely judged to be appropriate. Comments generated by artificial intelligence seem to be appearing progressively and represent approximately 3-4% in 2026. The removal of poor ratings appears to be marginal. Conclusions: Community pharmacists regularly and appropriately respond to online reviews, including, and in particular, less positive ones. These results could serve in the development of specific professional recommendations aimed at securing this practice.

title: A Two-Stage YOLO-Swin Transformer Pipeline for Cross-Dataset White Blood Cell Classification
desc: Background: White blood cell (WBC) classification across datasets is challenged by differences in staining, image context, and class distributions. Methods: We developed a two-stage YOLO11-Swin Transformer pipeline. In the first stage, WBC detection and context-preserving cropping, a YOLO11 detector finds the leukocyte in each uncropped image and produces a cell-focused crop that retains the surrounding background. In the second stage, WBC classification, a Swin Transformer (Swin-B) assigns the crop to one of nine cell types. The classifier was trained on detector-cropped cells from five public datasets, so the first stage supplies the same kind of input at test time; morphology-preserving color augmentation addressed staining variation, and class-weighted cross-entropy addressed class imbalance. WBCBench2026, a public benchmark not used for training, served for external evaluation in seven harmonized classes, scored by macro-F1 (the mean of per-class F1). Further analyses removed the first stage or masked the background, compared classifier backbones, held out each training dataset (leave-one-dataset-out, LODO), and tested a second split (Phase-2) with about 60% synthetically degraded images. Results: The full pipeline reached an external macro-F1 of 0.879{+/-}0.006 on 8,080 benchmark images. With uncropped images as input, the same crop-trained classifier reached 0.627{+/-}0.039, and crops that kept the surrounding background outperformed background-masked crops (0.867 versus 0.760). With identical detector-cropped input, Swin-B outperformed convolutional baselines (0.863 versus 0.718-0.813), and its advantage over ResNet50 persisted across three training configurations. In LODO, macro-F1 on the held-out dataset ranged from 0.59 to 0.91, revealing source-specific variation not fully covered by the remaining datasets. On Phase-2, macro-F1 was 0.769{+/-}0.002. Two hematologists independently reviewed all 205 blast- or promyelocyte-related model-benchmark disagreements and gave the same verdict on 73 crops (35.6%): 21 model right, 43 model wrong, 9 ambiguous. Conclusions: The proposed two-stage pipeline achieved strong cross-dataset WBC classification performance. Context-preserving cropping was essential for the crop-trained classifier, and the LODO findings support representing the same classes across diverse sources when developing robust WBC classifiers.

Targeting protein degradation strategies in drug discovery: integrating PROTACs, ubiquitination biology, and AI-driven design.
desc: [Molecular biomedicine] Targeted protein degradation (TPD) has emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy for eliminating disease-associated proteins, including targets that remain challenging to modulate using conventional occupancy-driven inhibitors. Among TPD approaches, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) exploit the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) to induce selective and event-driven degradation of proteins of interest (POIs). Despite rapid advances in PROTAC development, successful translation depends on interconnected determinants, including target degradability, ubiquitin ligase (E3) recruitment, warhead and linker properties, ternary-complex formation, ubiquitination efficiency, intracellular exposure, and pharmacokinetic behavior. This review provides an integrated, mechanism-oriented analysis of these determinants by linking PROTAC design, ubiquitination biology, computational approaches, and clinical development. We examine key principles governing PROTAC-mediated degradation, with emphasis on E3-ligase selection, linker design, ternary-complex geometry and cooperativity, ubiquitin (Ub)-acceptor lysine (Lys) accessibility, ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2)/E3 context, proteasomal engagement, inefficient degradation, and the hook effect. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning for degradation-activity prediction, E3-ligase/POI pairing, ligand and linker optimization, ternary-complex modeling, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) assessment are critically evaluated alongside their technical and translational limitations. Preclinical developments, clinical-stage degraders, emerging TPD modalities, and major barriers to translation are also discussed. We propose an integrated framework linking distinct target ubiquitination patterns, degrader design, ternary-complex geometry, AI-enabled prediction, and pharmacokinetic/clinical constraints, providing a mechanism-informed roadmap for the rational development of next-generation protein degraders and identifying mechanistic bottlenecks and translational priorities across therapeutic settings.

title: On the Creation of Object-Centric Event Logs from Patient Journeys
desc: Interactions between patients and health systems as well as conditions that individuals experience during a disease are represented in patient journeys. Therefore, patient journeys are important assets to investigate how care is being provided, and how health systems can be designed to better suit the needs of patients. While there is initial work on patient journeys from a process mining perspective with traditional case notions, object-centric process mining techniques have yet to be covered. This is unfortunate, since due to the rich structure of objects and their relationships, object-centric process mining approaches are particularly promising in this context. This paper addresses this gap by investigating object-centric event log (OCEL) generation from patient journeys. Based on a list of challenges and requirements, the paper presents an approach for the creation of OCELs from patient journey data. The approach is evaluated on a synthetic patient cohort provided by our industry partner.

Beyond the Chatbot: Agentic Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Infectious Disease Practice.
source: PubMed · Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America
desc: [Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America] Artificial intelligence (AI) discourse in infectious disease (ID) has focused on benchmarking large language model chatbots against clinicians, a useful but narrowing inquiry. Agentic AI is a different paradigm: goal-directed systems that pursue clinical objectives over time, integrating data, invoking tools, monitoring results, and adapting without repeated prompting. This Viewpoint defines the anatomy of an agent, situates it within a 3-level framework (predictive, conversational, agentic), and examines how agents could transform 6 domains of ID practice: clinical care, antimicrobial stewardship, clinical microbiology, infection prevention and control, research, and epidemiology and pandemic preparedness. Individual components have proven value; integrated systems remain untested. No validated agentic system has been deployed in clinical ID; error propagation, algorithmic bias, cost, absent validation frameworks, undefined liability, and consequences for the workforce and its training must be addressed first. The ID community has a narrow window to shape these systems before decisions are made without it.

title: FedTumor-IoMT: Federated Learning-Aided Brain Tumor Diagnosis on Resource-Constrained Edge IoMT Devices
desc: Joint brain tumor segmentation and classification models are computationally intensive, limiting their training on resource-constrained edge platforms and restricting privacy-preserving Federated Learning FL in the Internet of Medical Things IoMT. Existing approaches either perform both tasks on GPU-equipped workstations or support only classification on edge devices. To address this gap, this work proposes a lightweight multitask FL framework for joint segmentation and classification through local edge training. A shared pretrained LiteMedSAM encoder with TinyViT extracts features for a coordinate-attention-based segmentation decoder and a segmentation-guided classification head, eliminating a separate feature extractor. Selective encoder freezing retains 95\% trainable parameters while reducing on-device training costs. The proposed framework is experimentally validated on a laboratory testbed of five resource-constrained edge clients using 1,200 T1-weighted MRI samples. It achieves 94.20\% classification accuracy, 88.53\% DSC, 83.68\% IoU, and 99.87\% ROC-AUC. Its classification accuracy remains within 0.6\% of the GPU-trained baseline of 95.21\% across five FL rounds. The attention and feature refinement modules improve DSC and IoU by 3.82\% and 4.60\%, respectively, with 0.74 GFLOPs of additional computation. On edge hardware, the framework achieves 46.54 s inference latency, 52.8\% CPU utilization, and a peak temperature of 65$^\circ$C without thermal throttling. Its inference latency is observed to be 6.4--10.5 times lower than that of existing frameworks. These results demonstrate the feasibility of privacy-preserving joint brain tumor segmentation and classification on resource-constrained edge platforms.
