title: Medical Image Segmentation Is Now Just Another Coding Task
desc: For decades, every new medical image segmentation task has needed an expert, a dedicated architecture, and a framework such as nnU-Net. This is no longer the case: medical image segmentation is now just another coding task. Given only a task description, labeled data, and a CPU (with no segmentation framework, no pretrained weights, and no human in the loop), four off-the-shelf coding agents built segmenters for 13 tasks across four imaging modalities within hours, an ability that has emerged rather than been built. On the nine 2D tasks, their best programs reach 99% of the Dice of a GPU-trained nnU-Net. Like any code, a segmenter improves by being revised and checked, so we ask how far the same agents can improve their own segmentations and what unlocks further gains. On unseen cases there is no reference, so the agents inspect renderings of their own predictions: this alone lifts the worst tenth of cases by 0.09 Dice and cuts boundary error (HD95) by almost a quarter. Far more is within reach. Told the true Dice of each attempt, the same agents improve in all 14 matched pairs, rescue 85% of failed masks instead of 30%, and surpass the GPU-trained nnU-Net on average, by producing better masks rather than by choosing among them. What unlocks these gains is a quality signal, which neither visual inspection, nor more rounds, nor a quality estimator trained by the agents themselves yet supplies: we call this the quality blind spot. The ability to build and to repair is already present; the next advance will come not from another segmentation model, but from reference-free quality estimation that coding agents can call.

title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
desc: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.

title: CrownFusion: 3D Dental Crown Generation Using Geometry Images and Latent Diffusion
desc: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.

title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
desc: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

title: Engineering peptide-based drug delivery systems for cancer therapy: mechanisms, immunomodulation, and clinical translation.
desc: [Medical oncology (Northwood, London, England)] The clinical effectiveness of conventional cancer chemotherapy is often compromised by insufficient tumor specificity, dose-limiting systemic toxicity, poor intratumoral penetration, and the emergence of therapeutic resistance. Peptide-based drug-delivery platforms have attracted increasing attention as adaptable tools to overcome these challenges, as peptides can serve as tumor-targeting ligands, cell-penetrating moieties, bioactive therapeutic agents, cleavable linkers, and self-assembling structural units. This review provides an overview of the key characteristics of therapeutic peptides and critically evaluates their use in the delivery of major categories of anticancer drugs, including alkylating agents, platinum-based compounds, antimetabolites, antitumor antibiotics, topoisomerase inhibitors, mitotic inhibitors, and naturally derived therapeutics. Particular attention is given to peptide-drug conjugates, peptide-modified liposomes and nanoparticles, supramolecular nanostructures, hydrogels, and stimuli-responsive delivery systems, with emphasis on their capacity to improve tumor targeting, cellular uptake, controlled drug release, tissue penetration, and resistance reversal. The review further examines the immunoregulatory potential of peptide-enabled drug-delivery systems, including their ability to modulate tumor-associated macrophages, autophagy, NF-κB signaling, apoptotic pathways, and immunogenic cell death, thereby promoting coordinated innate and adaptive antitumor responses. Emerging clinical findings involving peptide vaccines and brain-penetrating peptide-drug conjugates further highlight their translational potential. Nevertheless, broader clinical implementation is still hindered by proteolytic degradation, rapid systemic elimination, tumor and receptor heterogeneity, protein-corona formation, nonspecific accumulation, manufacturing challenges, and insufficient standardization. Strategies such as peptide cyclization, incorporation of non-natural amino acids, PEGylation, optimization of ligand density, stimuli-sensitive linkers, multivalent targeting, biomarker-driven patient stratification, and scalable quality-controlled manufacturing may help overcome these barriers. Moreover, artificial intelligence and machine learning could facilitate peptide sequence optimization and rational platform design, although their successful application requires standardized datasets, interpretable predictive models, and rigorous prospective validation.

title: LingSante MedGuard Technical Report
desc: As medical AI is increasingly used for patient consultation and clinical decision support, identifying harmful, non-compliant, or ethically problematic responses is essential for responsible deployment. Assessing these risks requires checking clinical claims against relevant evidence, verifying calculations, and applying medical requirements under their intended conditions. We introduce LingSante MedGuard, a capability-enhanced guardrail that integrates supervision from a medical guardrail teacher model and six specialized medical capability experts into a unified model. The guardrail teacher supervises risk decisions and explanations across medical safety, compliance, and ethics, while the capability experts support medical rule understanding, numerical reasoning, multimodal hallucination detection, agentic safety verification, risk localization, and multimodal entity understanding. We consolidate these sources of supervision through offline supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated demonstrations, followed by multi-teacher on-policy distillation using feedback on student-generated responses. We further introduce LingSante MedGuardBench, a benchmark comprising 11 risk-detection subsets spanning medical safety, compliance, and ethics. At 4B, 9B, and 27B scales, LingSante MedGuard achieves mean benchmark F1 scores of 82.3%, 82.4%, and 87.4%, respectively. The 4B model also achieves 73.9% mean accuracy across MedHallu and MedHALT-NOTA under retrieval-enabled evaluation. Additional evaluations of the verification components show improvements in evidence-supported consistency, source traceability, and rule-guided rationale quality across model scales. These results support the integration of specialized medical capabilities into a unified guardrail for medical risk assessment and evidence-based medical safety verification.

title: Reducing Demographic Bias in Medical Imaging Using Siamese Representation Learning.
source: PubMed · Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
desc: [Journal of imaging informatics in medicine] Deep learning models for medical imaging often exhibit demographic bias, leading to performance disparities across protected groups such as age, gender, and race. This study proposes a debiasing framework to reduce such disparities while maintaining diagnostic accuracy. We propose a Siamese neural network trained using triplet loss, where demographic attributes are incorporated into triplet selection to encourage separation by disease class while promoting within-class similarity across demographic groups. The method was evaluated on pleural effusion detection using chest X-rays (109,005 images from 41,063 patients) and Alzheimer's disease classification using brain MRI (1494 scans from 348 patients). Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), precision, and true positive rate, along with equalized odds difference. The proposed method significantly reduced demographic disparities while maintaining or improving overall predictive performance compared with baseline and existing debiasing approaches. In pleural effusion detection, true positive rate gaps were reduced by 32% (race), 8% (age), and 22% (gender). In Alzheimer's disease classification, the true positive rate gap was reduced by 41% (age). Model interpretation indicated clinically meaningful imaging features were used for decision-making. Demographic-aware triplet sampling within a Siamese framework can effectively mitigate demographic performance disparities in medical imaging models while maintaining competitive overall diagnostic performance, suggesting potential for more equitable and clinically reliable deployment of medical imaging AI systems.

Transitions of Care in Clinical Oncology: Current Applications and Future Opportunities Enabled by Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health.
desc: [JCO clinical cancer informatics] Transitions of care from hospital to outpatient settings represent a vulnerable period for patients with cancer, who often face complex treatment regimens, multiple comorbidities, and fragmented coordination across care settings. These challenges contribute to communication breakdowns and unplanned hospital readmissions. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health technologies offer new opportunities to improve the transitional phases before, during, and after hospital discharge, and strengthen care continuity. This review examines emerging approaches enabled by AI and digital health across the inpatient-to-outpatient care spectrum for hospitalized patients with cancer. We discuss how predictive analytics and clinical decision support can identify patients at elevated risk of complications and guide discharge planning before hospitalization ends. We also review existing AI and digital health solutions tailored to the discharge process, including tools that enhance patient and caregiver education, medication reconciliation, follow-up coordination, discharge documentation, and management of pending test results. Finally, we explore post-discharge technologies, such as remote monitoring, symptom tracking systems, and AI-assisted communication platforms, that empower earlier detection of clinical deterioration and facilitate integration with outpatient and community-based resources. Overall, we highlight, as well as describe the limitations of, innovations that seek to improve coordination, reduce administrative burden, and support safer, more proactive transitions of care for patients undergoing cancer treatment.

title: Rethinking radiation dose optimization in pediatric computed tomography imaging: emerging algorithms and clinical integration.
desc: [Pediatric radiology] The optimization of radiation dose in pediatric computed tomography (CT) is a critical imperative, driven by the heightened radiosensitivity of children. This review provides a critical analysis of the evolution of dose optimization, from foundational principles like As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) and conventional techniques to the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI). We trace the progression from iterative reconstruction (IR), which offered initial dose reduction but was limited by unnatural image textures and computational demands, to the new paradigm of deep learning reconstruction (DLR) and emerging detector technologies like photon-counting CT. Clinical evidence demonstrates that DLR significantly shifts the traditional compromise between dose and image quality, enabling substantial potential dose reductions while producing images with superior noise properties and diagnostic confidence. Beyond reconstruction, AI is also automating scan protocoling to enhance consistency and reduce errors. However, the clinical integration of these powerful tools is not seamless. Significant barriers remain, including the "black box" nature of algorithms, the need for new training curricula for radiographers, and complex ethical and regulatory challenges. This review synthesizes these issues and charts a path forward, advocating for a holistic approach involving complementary AI-specific reference levels, federated learning, and robust governance to realize the full potential of a safer, more efficient, and patient-specific dose optimization ecosystem.

title: Immunomodulatory peptides for cancer therapy: mechanisms, applications, and precision immunotherapy.
desc: [Experimental hematology & oncology] Cancer immunotherapy, a pivotal element of precision medicine, has notably reshaped treatment paradigms in oncology. Peptide-based agents are emerging as powerful tools in antitumor immunotherapy due to their unique pharmacodynamic profiles, including compact size, enhanced tissue permeability, low immunogenicity, precise targeting, and versatile modifiability. Functionally, these peptides orchestrate multimodal immunomodulatory effects through (1) binding with high affinity to immune cell surface receptors, enabling precision immune engineering, (2) augmenting immune effector functions, (3) reprogramming the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), and (4) synergizing with conventional therapies or immune checkpoint modulators. This review comprehensively outlines the mechanisms and therapeutic applications of immunomodulatory peptides across diverse immune cell types, such as T cells, B cells, natural killer/natural killer T (NK/NKT) cells, macrophages, dendritic cells (DCs), neutrophils, and mast cells, with an emphasis on signal transduction regulation. Although challenges, including short half-lives, off-target effects, patient heterogeneity, and immunogenicity, remain, innovative engineering strategies such as structural cyclization and fatty acid conjugation have substantially improved metabolic stability and targeting accuracy. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with multiomics platforms is further accelerating target discovery and enabling the design of patient-specific peptides. This review summarizes current understanding of immunomodulatory peptides in cancer therapy, outlines their mechanisms of action and design considerations, and discusses ongoing efforts in AI-assisted peptide discovery, personalized neoantigen vaccine development, and advanced delivery systems.

title: EffNetV2M-ViT: A Hybrid Deep Learning Model for MRI-Based Differentiation of Glioblastoma and Brain Metastasis.
desc: [NMR in biomedicine] Noninvasive differentiation between glioblastoma (GBM) and brain metastasis (BM) remains challenging because of substantial overlap in their MRI appearance. Existing deep learning (DL) approaches have primarily relied on either convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which capture local spatial features, or transformer-based models, which capture long-range contextual relationships. However, the complementary value of combining these representations for GBM-BM discrimination has not been sufficiently investigated, using independently validated multicenter data. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a hybrid CNN-Vision Transformer (ViT) framework for automated differentiation of GBM from BM. The framework integrates EfficientNet-based convolutional feature extraction with ViT-based global feature modeling through parallel fusion. Enhancing tumor was automatically segmented using 3D U-Net, with segmentations visually reviewed and manually corrected when necessary. T2-weighted (T2W) and contrast enhanced T1-weighted (CE-T1W) MRI sequences were used as inputs. A modality ablation study was performed to identify the optimal contrast combination among T1W, CE-T1W, T2W, and FLAIR. The framework was evaluated in a retrospective cohort of 344 patients with histologically confirmed tumors using cross-validation and ensemble methods, with performance further assessed in an independent multicenter external validation cohort from different institutions, MRI scanner platforms, and patient populations. The hybrid EffNetV2M-ViT framework achieved an accuracy of 95.4%, F1-score of 96.2%, and AUC of 98.4% on the internal test set, and 90.9%, 92.7%, and 96.8% on external validation, with sensitivity, specificity of 96.2%, 93.9% and 90.5%, 91.7%, respectively. The hybrid model outperformed the standalone CNN and ViT models across both datasets, with the largest performance gains observed in the external validation cohort, support its generalizability. Ablation analysis confirmed that the paired CE-T1W + T2W input yielded the most consistent performance across both cohorts, with additional contrasts providing no added benefit. These findings suggest that combining local convolutional features with global contextual representations improves automated GBM-BM discrimination, offering a noninvasive, standardized approach for MRI-based tumor classification that may support clinical decision-making.

title: Multimodal AI is Advancing Biomarker Discovery in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's Disease: Evidence, Limitations, and the Translational Gap.
desc: [Biomarker insights] Artificial intelligence is rapidly expanding the biomarker landscape for Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases. Multimodal systems combining neuroimaging, speech, gait, physiological signals, cognitive measures, and molecular markers show substantial research-stage performance. In studies with extractable accuracy and denominator data, reported Parkinson's disease classification accuracies ranged from 94.25% (95% Wilson CI: 93.78-94.68%) to 98.6% (95% Wilson CI: 95.71-99.67%), while Alzheimer's disease diagnostic or conversion-prediction accuracies ranged from 65.8% (95% Wilson CI: 62.54-68.87%) to 99.26% (95% Wilson CI: 97.89-99.75%). Therefore, the field is no longer limited by the absence of candidate AI biomarkers. However, the central bottleneck is translational validation. External validation remains uncommon across medical AI, with rates of 3.7% in high-impact medical informatics studies, 6% in diagnostic medical-imaging AI studies, and 14.7% in ICU AI scoring-system studies. In neurodegenerative disease, many models still rely on single cohorts, internal splits, incomplete metric reporting, and weak linkage between AI-derived digital phenotypes and established molecular or clinical biomarkers. Consequently, performance degradation in real-world populations, reduced specificity, calibration drift, and cohort bias help explain why extensive machine learning activity has not yet translated into routine clinical deployment. In this narrative review, we therefore synthesize quantitative evidence across motor, cognitive, neuropsychiatric, remote-monitoring, and neuroimaging domains. We argue that progress in AI for Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease now depends less on additional model novelty alone than on standardized validation pipelines, external cohort testing, calibration assessment, interpretable multimodal fusion, and clinically meaningful endpoints. Nonetheless, with these safeguards, multimodal AI can move from promising biomarker discovery toward reproducible, clinically deployable precision diagnostics in neurodegenerative disease.

title: Ultrasound-responsive microbubble platforms in lung cancer: mechanisms, molecular targeting, and therapeutic applications.
source: PubMed · Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
desc: [Frontiers in cell and developmental biology] Lung cancer remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality, while the heterogeneous tumor microenvironment, abnormal vasculature, elevated interstitial fluid pressure, hypoxia, and dense extracellular matrix substantially limit the efficacy of conventional systemic therapies. Ultrasound-responsive microbubbles (MBs) have emerged as versatile theranostic platforms capable of overcoming several of these delivery barriers through externally controlled acoustic cavitation. This review comprehensively discusses the evolution, physicochemical characteristics, composition, and functional mechanisms of MB-based systems for lung cancer diagnosis and therapy. Particular emphasis is placed on stable and inertial cavitation, sonoporation, microstreaming, vascular permeabilization, and enhanced transport of therapeutic agents into tumor tissue. The diagnostic potential of targeted MBs for contrast-enhanced ultrasound, molecular imaging, perfusion assessment, and super-resolution visualization of tumor vasculature is highlighted. Therapeutic applications encompassing chemotherapeutics, nucleic acids, microRNAs, oxygen delivery, immunotherapy, and combination strategies with radiotherapy are critically examined. The review also discusses molecularly targeted MBs, nanoparticle-MB hybrids, and ultrasound-triggered modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment. Despite promising preclinical outcomes, challenges involving pulmonary acoustic attenuation, short circulation time, biodistribution, treatment parameter standardization, manufacturing, safety, and regulatory requirements remain. Emerging theranostic, hybrid, and artificial intelligence-assisted platforms may facilitate personalized and clinically translatable microbubble-based precision therapy for lung cancer.

title: An Integrated Systems Biology and Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Robust Placental Biomarker Discovery in Preeclampsia.
source: PubMed · FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
desc: [FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology] Preeclampsia (PE) is a heterogeneous pregnancy disorder characterized by placental dysfunction and immune dysregulation. Translation of transcriptomic biomarkers has been limited by inconsistent feature selection, inadequate external validation, and poor model interpretability. We developed an explainable, externally validated, transcriptomics-driven artificial intelligence framework for biomarker discovery, PE diagnosis, and exploratory severity stratification. Placental transcriptomic datasets were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus. Differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis were integrated with consensus feature selection using Elastic Net, LASSO, SVM-RFE, and Boruta. Selected biomarkers were evaluated using conventional machine learning, deep learning, ensemble, and hybrid models with repeated stratified cross-validation and independent cross-platform external validation. Model performance and interpretability were assessed using ROC and precision-recall analyses, DeLong's test, permutation testing, SHAP, and permutation importance. Integrative analyses identified 166 candidate genes and prioritized a six-gene signature comprising CGB5, LEP, LIMCH1, LRRC1, PAPPA2, and SIGLEC6. Logistic Regression achieved the highest external performance (ROC-AUC: 0.8516, 95% CI: 0.7913-0.9119; PR-AUC: 0.8572). DeLong's test showed no significant differences from the best-performing deep or hybrid models. Explainability analyses consistently identified LEP, LRRC1, PAPPA2, and SIGLEC6 as major predictive contributors. Exploratory early versus late-onset PE stratification achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.7617. The proposed framework identified a reproducible six-gene placental signature with robust cross-platform predictive performance and biological interpretability. Integrating consensus biomarker selection, external validation, and explainable artificial intelligence may facilitate the reproducible development of transcriptomic biomarkers for precision medicine in PE.
